    1. Introduction

    In modern preventive healthcare and personal wellness management, dietary intake and nutrient balance play a pivotal role. The widespread availability of processed foods, irregular eating routines, and diverging nutritional needs across individuals have created an urgent imperative for structured dietary tracking systems. Many individuals attempt to monitor their caloric and macronutrient intake (proteins, carbohydrates, fats) using manual logbooks, generic smartphone note apps, or disconnected spreadsheets. However, manual recording systems quickly deteriorate: mathematical aggregation is labor-intensive, multi-item meals are recorded with varying serving definitions, and longitudinal history becomes fragmented or lost.

    NutriGuide — Your Personal Nutrition Companion is a comprehensive, production-grade relational database management system designed to systematically capture, organize, analyze, and optimize personal nutrition data. Engineered specifically for academic evaluation and clinical-demonstration rigor under the Database Management Systems (DBMS) curriculum, NutriGuide provides an enterprise-quality relational backend running on the MySQL 8.x relational database engine with InnoDB ACID transactional semantics.

    The database models ten tightly integrated entities spanning:

  • User Demographics & Anthropometrics: Secure user credentials, demographic parameters (age, gender), physical measurements (height in centimeters, weight in kilograms), and physical activity levels.
  • Macronutrient & Caloric Target Goals: User-defined nutritional targets (calories, protein, carbohydrates, fat) with historical versioning and single-active-goal business rule enforcement.
  • Reference Food Catalog: Categorized food items (Grains, Proteins, Dairy, Fruits, Vegetables) with precise nutritional densities per standard serving size.
  • Multi-Item Meal Transactions: Real-time logging of breakfast, lunch, dinner, and snack meal events, resolved atomically through an associative junction entity (meal_item).
  • Prospective Meal Planning: Weekly and monthly diet regimens scheduled across date intervals, linked to designated target meal slots.
  • Rule-Based Recommendation History: Persisted dietary advisory guidelines evaluating user caloric deficits, surpluses, and protein compliance against standard WHO nutritional benchmarks.
  • Automated Audit Logging: Real-time audit trails maintained via database triggers capturing user operations without application-side overhead.

    • The core relational database is implemented in MySQL 8.x, enforcing schema stability through primary keys, foreign keys with explicit referential integrity actions (ON UPDATE CASCADE, ON DELETE CASCADE, ON DELETE RESTRICT), candidate key uniqueness, and declarative CHECK constraints. Above the table storage layer, NutriGuide incorporates high-level database programmability including stored functions for dynamic Body Mass Index (BMI) computation, stored procedures with output parameters for aggregate daily nutrition summaries, analytical views, and audit/validation triggers.

    2. Problem Statement (Step 1)

    Individuals and dietary consultants seeking to manage nutritional health through manual record-keeping face several systematic data management challenges:

  • Scattered and Disorganized Records: Dietary intake, body weight fluctuations, target goals, and food nutrient values are frequently noted in disparate physical notebooks, phone memos, or isolated spreadsheets. As a result, compiling a consolidated, longitudinal picture of an individual's nutritional health is virtually impossible.
  • Nutrient Calculation Errors & Latency: Computing cumulative daily calories and macro splits (grams of protein, carbohydrates, and fats) requires repetitive arithmetic scaling based on portion size. Manual calculations are prone to severe calculation errors, misleading users regarding their actual intake.
  • Data Redundancy & Inconsistency (Flat File Flaws): When nutritional data is stored in unnormalized flat files, food descriptions and nutrient densities are repeatedly duplicated across every logged meal. If the nutritional profile of an item (e.g., Cooked White Rice) is updated, records in earlier rows remain unchanged, creating contradictory records.
  • Lack of Validation & Boundary Integrity: Manual systems fail to prevent erroneous inputs such as negative serving sizes, negative weights or heights, or impossible calorie amounts.
  • Absence of Transactional Atomicity: A meal typically consists of multiple foods consumed together. In traditional spreadsheets, a partial crash during entry leaves orphaned records where a meal is recorded without its accompanying food components.
  • No Automated Audit History: Manual systems provide no reliable mechanism to detect when a meal was logged, modified, or deleted, impeding auditability and compliance tracking.
  • Disconnected Goal Analysis: Without automated relational joins between logged intake and active goals, users cannot deterministically evaluate whether they are in a caloric surplus or deficit.

    • Proposed Solution

    NutriGuide resolves each of these challenges through a centralized, strictly normalized relational database. The schema eliminates data redundancy, guarantees referential and transactional integrity, automates dynamic metric calculations through stored subprograms, enforces data validation at the storage layer via CHECK constraints and triggers, and enables instantaneous reporting through pre-aggregated SQL views.

    3. System Architecture and Modules

    3.1 Three-Tier Relational Topology

    The NutriGuide architecture is structured into three clean, decoupled tiers:

  • Presentation Layer (Java Swing Client): An ergonomic Windows desktop user interface built using Java Swing. It provides dedicated user interface windows (LoginFrame, RegisterFrame, DashboardFrame, MealLogFrame, NutritionGoalFrame, RecommendationFrame, ReportFrame, ProfileFrame) running on the Swing Event Dispatch Thread (EDT). All long-running API operations are dispatched asynchronously using SwingWorker threads to prevent user interface freezing.
  • Application & Logic Layer (Java HttpServer): A lightweight, high-performance HTTP REST server running on http://127.0.0.1:8081. It encapsulates the application services (AuthenticationService, NutritionService, MealService, FoodService, RecommendationService, ReportService, UserService), token-based SessionManager, and salted PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 password security. It issues parameterized JDBC queries to MySQL.
  • Relational Database Layer (MySQL 8.x Engine): The relational database tier manages table storage using the InnoDB storage engine. It provides ACID transactional guarantees, enforces relational integrity, executes stored functions and procedures, maintains aggregation views, and automatically invokes audit and validation triggers.

    • Figure 3.1: System Architecture

    Figure 3.1: NutriGuide System Architecture & Multi-Tier Topology

    3.2 System Modules

  • User Profile & Authentication Module (user_profile):
  • Manages user account intake, authentication, and secure demographic tracking.
  • Stores user height, weight, age, gender, and physical activity tier.
  • Protects user credentials using salted PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 password digests with an adaptive 600,000-iteration work factor.
  • Nutrition Goal Management Module (nutrition_goal):
  • Allows users to configure custom daily caloric and macronutrient targets.
  • Implements historical versioning through an is_active status flag.
  • Enforces the business constraint that exactly one goal may remain active per user at any given timestamp.
  • Food Catalog & Categorization Module (food_category, food):
  • Maintains a standardized, immutable reference catalog of foods classified into primary dietary groups (Grains, Proteins, Dairy, Fruits, Vegetables).
  • Tracks standard serving sizes in grams and associated energy/macronutrient values (calories, protein, carbs, fat).
  • Meal Logging & Transaction Module (meal, meal_item):
  • Captures daily meal events (Breakfast, Lunch, Dinner, Snack).
  • Utilizes an associative junction entity (meal_item) to resolve the many-to-many relationship between meals and food items.
  • Enforces ACID transactions with atomic commit and rollback capabilities.
  • Meal Planning Module (meal_plan, meal_plan_item):
  • Enables prospective diet regimen scheduling across structured date windows (e.g., 7-day weight cut plan, 30-day muscle gain plan).
  • Resolves planned meal schedules against food catalog entries.
  • Rule-Based Recommendation Engine (recommendation):
  • Evaluates active nutritional goals against actual aggregate daily intake.
  • Deterministically generates clinically grounded educational guidance regarding caloric deficits, surpluses, and protein adequacy.
  • Automated Audit & Logging Module (activity_log):
  • Maintains a tamper-evident audit history of user lifecycle actions and trigger-logged meal transactions.
  • Reporting & Analytics Module (views, procedures):
  • Leverages SQL views (daily_nutrition_summary, food_category_details) and stored procedures (get_daily_summary) to generate instantaneous analytical reports for date ranges.

    4.1 Functional Requirements

    Requirement ID Functional Description Implemented Database Object
    FR1 Store and retrieve user profiles including height, weight, age, gender, and activity level. Table `user_profile`
    FR2 Securely hash user passwords using salted PBKDF2 with 600,000 iterations; prevent plaintext leakage. Table `user_profile.password_hash`, `PasswordUtil.java`
    FR3 Enforce global uniqueness of user email addresses to prevent duplicate registrations. Constraint `UNIQUE KEY uq_user_email` on `user_profile`
    FR4 Maintain food categories to systematically classify nutritional catalog items. Table `food_category`
    FR5 Store verified food items with per-serving caloric, protein, carbohydrate, and fat densities. Table `food` (FK `category_id`)
    FR6 Enforce uniqueness of food names to avoid duplicate food item creation. Constraint `UNIQUE KEY uq_food_name` on `food`
    FR7 Prevent physical deletion of food items referenced in past meal records to preserve historical integrity. Referential Action `ON DELETE RESTRICT` on `meal_item.food_id`
    FR8 Allow users to establish macronutrient and caloric target goals with historical archiving. Table `nutrition_goal`
    FR9 Enforce that only one nutrition goal is active (`is_active = TRUE`) per user account. Service Layer Transaction & Table `nutrition_goal`
    FR10 Record meal events linked to an authenticated user with meal type and date. Table `meal` (FK `user_id`)
    FR11 Atomically record multi-item meal lines linked to a parent meal and food catalog item. Table `meal_item` (Composite/Surrogate PK, FKs)
    FR12 Automatically log meal insertion events into the audit log without application intervention. Trigger `trg_after_meal_insert` on `meal`
    FR13 Reject invalid or non-positive food serving quantities at the database engine level. Trigger `trg_validate_meal_quantity` (SIGNAL '45000')
    FR14 Automatically compute user Body Mass Index (BMI) dynamically via a stored database function. Stored Function `calculate_bmi(weight_kg, height_cm)`
    FR15 Provide instantaneous multi-table aggregated daily nutritional intake totals. Relational View `daily_nutrition_summary`
    FR16 Return consolidated daily macro totals via stored procedure with output parameters. Stored Procedure `get_daily_summary(...)`
    FR17 Store prospective multi-day diet plans and their component planned meal items. Tables `meal_plan`, `meal_plan_item`
    FR18 Automatically clean up all dependent records (goals, meals, plans, logs) upon user profile deletion. Referential Action `ON DELETE CASCADE` across foreign keys

    4.2 Non-Functional Requirements

  • Data Integrity & Consistency: Enforce strict schema constraints including declarative PRIMARY KEYs, FOREIGN KEYs with explicit referential integrity rules, and CHECK constraints guarding against negative physical metrics.
  • ACID Transaction Compliance: Multi-item meal logging and goal transitions must execute within explicit atomic transaction boundaries with rollback on exception.
  • Precision of Nutritional Data: All caloric and macronutrient quantities must use high-precision fixed-point numeric types (DECIMAL(7,2), DECIMAL(6,2), DECIMAL(5,2)) instead of floating-point representations (FLOAT, DOUBLE) to prevent IEEE 754 rounding drift.
  • Architectural Security: The database binds strictly to local loops; passwords are never persisted or returned in plaintext; all SQL queries utilize parameterized statements to prevent SQL injection.
  • Modularity & High Cohesion: Schema separation strictly adheres to Third Normal Form (3NF), ensuring that tables correspond to discrete real-world business entities.

    Resolution of Many-to-Many Relationships

  • Meal and Food (M:N): A meal can consist of multiple foods (e.g., Rice, Dal, Salad), and a single food can be consumed across thousands of different meals. This M:N cardinality is decomposed into two 1:N relationships via the meal_item associative entity with quantity as an intersection attribute.
  • Meal_Plan and Food (M:N): A prospective diet plan contains multiple planned foods, and a food can be scheduled across numerous diet plans. This M:N relationship is resolved into two 1:N relationships via the meal_plan_item associative entity.

    8. Anomalies (Step 6)

    A database anomaly is a data integrity flaw that manifests when unrelated business facts are merged into a single unnormalized relation. To illustrate why NutriGuide must be decomposed into multiple normalized relations, consider an unnormalized "flat" design (NUTRITION_FLAT) where user profiles, meal events, food catalog attributes, and food categories are merged into a single table:

    Unnormalized Relation: `NUTRITION_FLAT`

    (Composite Candidate Key: {email, meal_date, meal_type, food_name})

    user_id name email height_cm weight_kg meal_date meal_type food_name serving_size calories protein category_name quantity
    1 John Doe user@example.com 175.00 70.00 2026-10-18 Lunch Grilled Chicken 100.00 165.00 31.00 Proteins 1.00
    1 John Doe user@example.com 175.00 70.00 2026-10-18 Lunch Cooked White Rice 100.00 130.00 2.70 Grains 1.50
    1 John Doe user@example.com 175.00 70.00 2026-10-18 Dinner Yellow Dal 100.00 116.00 7.30 Proteins 1.00
    2 Jane Smith jane@example.com 162.00 58.00 2026-10-18 Breakfast Rolled Oats 100.00 389.00 16.90 Grains 1.00

    8.1 Insertion Anomalies

  • Inability to Add Foods Without Meals: If a dietitian adds a newly certified food item (e.g., Broccoli) to the system, it cannot be inserted into NUTRITION_FLAT because user_id, email, meal_date, and meal_type form part of the candidate key and cannot be NULL.
  • Inability to Register New Users: A newly registered user cannot be stored until they log their first meal event, as food and meal attributes cannot be empty.
  • Inability to Create Food Categories: A new food category (e.g., Beverages) cannot be recorded unless an accompanying user, meal, and food item are simultaneously entered.

    • 8.2 Update Anomalies

  • Redundant User Attribute Updates: If John Doe updates his body weight from 70.00 kg to 68.50 kg, the update must be applied across every historical meal row he has ever logged. If an update statement updates only recent rows, John Doe will have contradictory weights in the database.
  • Food Nutritional Profile Changes: If the laboratory nutritional evaluation of Cooked White Rice updates its carbohydrate content, every past row referencing white rice must be modified. Incomplete updates lead to conflicting nutrient data.
  • Category Renaming Inconsistency: Renaming the category Proteins to Protein Sources requires searching and updating millions of meal item rows.

    • 8.3 Deletion Anomalies

  • Unintended Loss of User Data: If a user clears their meal history for a specific day, and that happens to be their only logged meal, deleting those rows completely purges their user profile, height, weight, and credentials from the system.
  • Unintended Loss of Food Catalog Items: If the only logged occurrence of Rolled Oats is deleted by Jane Smith, the entire nutritional profile of Rolled Oats and its category definition are permanently erased from the database.

    • 9. Functional Dependencies (Step 7)

    A functional dependency X → Y holds over a relation R if and only if whenever two tuples have identical values for X, they must also have identical values for Y.

    The formal functional dependencies governing the NutriGuide schema and their candidate keys are defined as follows:

    1. `user_profile`

  • Candidate Keys: {user_id}, {email}
  • Primary Key: user_id
  • Functional Dependencies:
  • user_id → name, email, password_hash, age, gender, height_cm, weight_kg, activity_level, created_at
  • email → user_id, name, password_hash, age, gender, height_cm, weight_kg, activity_level, created_at
  • Rationale: user_id uniquely identifies each user record. Because email is defined with a UNIQUE constraint, it also deterministically determines all attributes.

    • 2. `nutrition_goal`

  • Candidate Key: {goal_id}
  • Primary Key: goal_id
  • Functional Dependencies:
  • goal_id → user_id, target_calories, target_protein, target_carbs, target_fats, is_active, created_at
  • Rationale: Each configured goal is identified by its surrogate key goal_id.

    • 3. `food_category`

  • Candidate Keys: {category_id}, {category_name}
  • Primary Key: category_id
  • Functional Dependencies:
  • category_id → category_name
  • category_name → category_id
  • Rationale: Standard categories are uniquely identified by both numeric ID and unique textual name.

    • 4. `food`

  • Candidate Keys: {food_id}, {food_name}
  • Primary Key: food_id
  • Functional Dependencies:
  • food_id → category_id, food_name, serving_size, calories, protein, carbohydrates, fat
  • food_name → food_id, category_id, serving_size, calories, protein, carbohydrates, fat
  • Rationale: Nutritional facts are fixed per food item; either food_id or unique food_name determines all nutritional values.

    • 5. `meal`

  • Candidate Key: {meal_id}
  • Primary Key: meal_id
  • Functional Dependencies:
  • meal_id → user_id, meal_type, meal_date, created_at
  • Rationale: A meal event header is uniquely identified by meal_id. Multiple meals of the same type on the same date are supported (e.g., multiple snacks).

    • 6. `meal_item`

  • Candidate Keys: {meal_item_id}, {meal_id, food_id}
  • Primary Key: meal_item_id
  • Functional Dependencies:
  • meal_item_id → meal_id, food_id, quantity
  • (meal_id, food_id) → meal_item_id, quantity
  • Rationale: An individual meal line item references a specific portion quantity of a food within a meal event.

    • 7. `meal_plan`

  • Candidate Key: {meal_plan_id}
  • Primary Key: meal_plan_id
  • Functional Dependencies:
  • meal_plan_id → user_id, plan_name, start_date, end_date, is_active, created_at

    • 8. `meal_plan_item`

  • Candidate Key: {meal_plan_item_id}
  • Primary Key: meal_plan_item_id
  • Functional Dependencies:
  • meal_plan_item_id → meal_plan_id, food_id, planned_meal_type, quantity

    • 9. `recommendation`

  • Candidate Key: {rec_id}
  • Primary Key: rec_id
  • Functional Dependencies:
  • rec_id → user_id, rec_type, message, generated_at

    • 10. `activity_log`

  • Candidate Key: {log_id}
  • Primary Key: log_id
  • Functional Dependencies:
  • log_id → user_id, action_taken, log_time

    • 10. Normalization (Step 8: 1NF to BCNF)

    Normalization is the formal mathematical decomposition of relational schemas to eliminate redundancy and prevent the anomalies identified in Section 8. NutriGuide was engineered by decomposing the initial flat design progressively from 1NF through Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF).

    10.1 First Normal Form (1NF)

    Rule: A relation R is in 1NF if and only if all underlying domains contain only atomic (indivisible) values, and there are no repeating groups or multi-valued attributes.

  • Violation in Unnormalized Flat Design: In the unnormalized flat meal record, multiple food items and their respective portion quantities are grouped into comma-separated strings inside a single table cell (e.g., "Grilled Chicken, Cooked Rice" and "1.0, 1.5").

    • Figure 10.1: Before 1NF

    Figure 10.1: Before 1NF — Multi-valued repeating groups packed into single cells

  • 1NF Decomposition: Repeating groups are eliminated by decomposing the data into separate records where each cell holds exactly one atomic value. The parent meal header is isolated in meal, while individual food lines are stored in meal_item.

    • Figure 10.2: After 1NF

    Figure 10.2: After 1NF — Decomposed into meal and meal_item with strictly atomic attributes

    10.2 Second Normal Form (2NF)

    Rule: A relation R is in 2NF if and only if it is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on the entire primary key (no partial functional dependencies on proper subsets of candidate keys).

  • Violation in 1NF Composite Table: If we consider an associative relation combining (meal_id, food_id) as the composite key along with user attributes and food nutritional values:
  • (meal_id, food_id) → quantity (Full dependency on composite key)
  • food_id → food_name, serving_size, calories, protein (Partial dependency on proper subset food_id)
  • meal_id → user_id, meal_date (Partial dependency on proper subset meal_id)

    • Figure 10.3: Before 2NF

    Figure 10.3: Before 2NF — Partial dependencies on proper subsets of composite candidate key

  • 2NF Decomposition: The partially dependent attributes are extracted into independent relations:
  • food retains attributes determined solely by food_id.
  • meal retains attributes determined solely by meal_id.
  • meal_item retains only quantity, which requires the complete composite key (meal_id, food_id).

    • Figure 10.4: After 2NF

    Figure 10.4: After 2NF — Decomposed into relations where all non-key attributes are fully dependent on the primary key

    10.3 Third Normal Form (3NF)

    Rule: A relation R is in 3NF if and only if it is in 2NF and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on any candidate key (X → Y and Y → Z where Y is not a candidate key).

  • Violation in 2NF Food Table: In the food relation before 3NF, the category name is included directly alongside the category ID:
  • food_id → category_id
  • category_id → category_name
  • Therefore: food_id → category_name is a transitive dependency through non-candidate key category_id.

    • Figure 10.5: Before 3NF

    Figure 10.5: Before 3NF — Transitive dependency creates update and deletion anomalies

  • 3NF Decomposition: The transitive dependency is eliminated by extracting food_category into an independent reference table (category_id, category_name), leaving food with only the foreign key category_id.

    • Figure 10.6: After 3NF

    Figure 10.6: After 3NF — Transitive dependency eliminated by isolating food_category lookup entity

    10.4 Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)

    Rule: A relation R is in BCNF if and only if for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y, X is a superkey (candidate key).

    BCNF Verification for NutriGuide Relations:

  • In user_profile: Non-trivial dependencies have determinants user_id or email. Both are candidate keys. ✓
  • In food: Determinants are food_id and food_name. Both are unique candidate keys. ✓
  • In food_category: Determinants are category_id and category_name. Both are unique candidate keys. ✓
  • In nutrition_goal, meal, meal_item, meal_plan, meal_plan_item, recommendation, activity_log: Every determinant is a primary or candidate key. ✓

    • Conclusion: All ten relations in the NutriGuide schema strictly satisfy Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF).

    10.5 Decomposition Summary

    Unnormalized Flat Concept Normalized 3NF/BCNF Relations Primary Keys Foreign Keys
    User & Demographics `user_profile` `user_id` None
    Calorie & Macro Goals `nutrition_goal` `goal_id` `user_id`
    Food Categories `food_category` `category_id` None
    Reference Food Catalog `food` `food_id` `category_id`
    Meal Events Header `meal` `meal_id` `user_id`
    Meal Items (Multi-Item Lines) `meal_item` `meal_item_id` `meal_id`, `food_id`
    Prospective Diet Plans `meal_plan` `meal_plan_id` `user_id`
    Diet Plan Items `meal_plan_item` `meal_plan_item_id` `meal_plan_id`, `food_id`
    Recommendation History `recommendation` `rec_id` `user_id`
    System Audit Trail `activity_log` `log_id` `user_id`

    10.6 Lossless Join Verification

    To prove that the decomposition is mathematically lossless (no information is created or lost), the original flat meal record is reconstructed by joining the normalized relations:

    
SELECT 
    u.name AS user_name,
    m.meal_date,
    m.meal_type,
    f.food_name,
    c.category_name,
    mi.quantity,
    ROUND(f.calories * mi.quantity, 2) AS total_calories,
    ROUND(f.protein * mi.quantity, 2) AS total_protein
FROM meal m
JOIN user_profile u ON m.user_id = u.user_id
JOIN meal_item mi ON m.meal_id = mi.meal_id
JOIN food f ON mi.food_id = f.food_id
JOIN food_category c ON f.category_id = c.category_id
WHERE u.user_id = 1
ORDER BY m.meal_date, m.meal_id, mi.meal_item_id;

    Lossless Reconstruction Output:

    user_name meal_date meal_type food_name category_name quantity total_calories total_protein
    John Doe 2026-10-18 Lunch Grilled Chicken Breast Proteins 1.00 165.00 31.00
    John Doe 2026-10-18 Lunch Cooked White Rice Grains 1.50 195.00 4.05
    John Doe 2026-10-18 Dinner Yellow Dal (Cooked) Proteins 1.00 116.00 7.30
    John Doe 2026-10-18 Dinner Whole Wheat Roti Grains 2.00 240.00 7.00

    11. Implementation of Tables in MySQL (Step 9)

    The NutriGuide database is implemented in MySQL 8.x utilizing the ACID-compliant InnoDB storage engine. All declarative constraints (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT, NOT NULL) are enforced at the database kernel level.

    11.1 Table DDL Definitions

    
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS nutriguide;
USE nutriguide;

-- 1. USER_PROFILE
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS user_profile (
    user_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    password_hash VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    age INT NOT NULL CHECK (age > 0),
    gender VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    height_cm DECIMAL(5, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (height_cm > 0),
    weight_kg DECIMAL(5, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (weight_kg > 0),
    activity_level VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- 2. NUTRITION_GOAL
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS nutrition_goal (
    goal_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INT NOT NULL,
    target_calories DECIMAL(7, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (target_calories >= 0),
    target_protein DECIMAL(6, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (target_protein >= 0),
    target_carbs DECIMAL(6, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (target_carbs >= 0),
    target_fats DECIMAL(6, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (target_fats >= 0),
    is_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    CONSTRAINT fk_nutrition_goal_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
        REFERENCES user_profile (user_id)
        ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- 3. FOOD_CATEGORY
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS food_category (
    category_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    category_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- 4. FOOD
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS food (
    food_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    category_id INT NOT NULL,
    food_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    serving_size DECIMAL(6, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (serving_size > 0),
    calories DECIMAL(6, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (calories >= 0),
    protein DECIMAL(5, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (protein >= 0),
    carbohydrates DECIMAL(5, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (carbohydrates >= 0),
    fat DECIMAL(5, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (fat >= 0),
    CONSTRAINT fk_food_category FOREIGN KEY (category_id)
        REFERENCES food_category (category_id)
        ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- 5. MEAL
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS meal (
    meal_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INT NOT NULL,
    meal_type VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    meal_date DATE NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    CONSTRAINT fk_meal_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
        REFERENCES user_profile (user_id)
        ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- 6. MEAL_ITEM
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS meal_item (
    meal_item_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    meal_id INT NOT NULL,
    food_id INT NOT NULL,
    quantity DECIMAL(5, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
    CONSTRAINT fk_meal_item_meal FOREIGN KEY (meal_id)
        REFERENCES meal (meal_id)
        ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE,
    CONSTRAINT fk_meal_item_food FOREIGN KEY (food_id)
        REFERENCES food (food_id)
        ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- 7. MEAL_PLAN
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS meal_plan (
    meal_plan_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INT NOT NULL,
    plan_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    start_date DATE NOT NULL,
    end_date DATE NOT NULL,
    is_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    CONSTRAINT fk_meal_plan_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
        REFERENCES user_profile (user_id)
        ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- 8. MEAL_PLAN_ITEM
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS meal_plan_item (
    meal_plan_item_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    meal_plan_id INT NOT NULL,
    food_id INT NOT NULL,
    planned_meal_type VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    quantity DECIMAL(5, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
    CONSTRAINT fk_meal_plan_item_plan FOREIGN KEY (meal_plan_id)
        REFERENCES meal_plan (meal_plan_id)
        ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE,
    CONSTRAINT fk_meal_plan_item_food FOREIGN KEY (food_id)
        REFERENCES food (food_id)
        ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- 9. RECOMMENDATION
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS recommendation (
    rec_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INT NOT NULL,
    rec_type VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    message VARCHAR(500) NOT NULL,
    generated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    CONSTRAINT fk_recommendation_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
        REFERENCES user_profile (user_id)
        ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- 10. ACTIVITY_LOG
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS activity_log (
    log_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INT NOT NULL,
    action_taken VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    log_time TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    CONSTRAINT fk_activity_log_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
        REFERENCES user_profile (user_id)
        ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

    12. Functions, Procedures, Triggers and Queries (Step 10)

    12.1 Stored Functions (DBMS Exp 6)

    Function 1: `calculate_bmi(weight_kg, height_cm)`

  • Mathematical Formula: BMI = weight_kg / (height_m)² = weight_kg / (height_cm / 100)²
  • Determinism: Declared DETERMINISTIC NO SQL for maximum execution performance and compiler query caching.
    • 
DELIMITER $$
CREATE FUNCTION calculate_bmi(weight_kg DECIMAL(5, 2), height_cm DECIMAL(5, 2))
RETURNS DECIMAL(5, 2)
DETERMINISTIC
NO SQL
BEGIN
    DECLARE height_m DECIMAL(5, 4);
    DECLARE bmi DECIMAL(5, 2);

    IF height_cm IS NULL OR height_cm <= 0 OR weight_kg IS NULL OR weight_kg <= 0 THEN
        RETURN 0.00;
    END IF;

    SET height_m = height_cm / 100.0000;
    SET bmi = weight_kg / (height_m * height_m);

    RETURN ROUND(bmi, 2);
END $$
DELIMITER ;
    Test Execution:
    
SELECT 
    name, 
    height_cm, 
    weight_kg, 
    calculate_bmi(weight_kg, height_cm) AS calculated_bmi 
FROM user_profile;
    Output:
    name height_cm weight_kg calculated_bmi
    John Doe 175.00 70.00 22.86
    Jane Smith 162.00 58.00 22.10

    Function 2: `get_total_calories(user_id, meal_date)`

  • Purpose: Computes total caloric intake for a user on a given date by aggregating food calories scaled by portion quantities.
    • 
DELIMITER $$
CREATE FUNCTION get_total_calories(p_user_id INT, p_date DATE)
RETURNS DECIMAL(7, 2)
READS SQL DATA
BEGIN
    DECLARE total_cals DECIMAL(7, 2);

    SELECT COALESCE(SUM(f.calories * mi.quantity), 0.00)
    INTO total_cals
    FROM meal m
    JOIN meal_item mi ON m.meal_id = mi.meal_id
    JOIN food f ON mi.food_id = f.food_id
    WHERE m.user_id = p_user_id AND m.meal_date = p_date;

    RETURN total_cals;
END $$
DELIMITER ;
    Test Execution:
    
SELECT get_total_calories(1, '2026-10-18') AS john_total_calories;
    Output:
    john_total_calories
    1395.50

    12.2 Stored Procedures (DBMS Exp 7)

    Procedure: `get_daily_summary(p_user_id, p_date, OUT p_calories, OUT p_protein, OUT p_carbs, OUT p_fat)`

  • Purpose: Retrieves all four macronutrient totals for a user on a specific date using SQL OUT parameters.
    • 
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE get_daily_summary(
    IN p_user_id INT,
    IN p_date DATE,
    OUT p_calories DECIMAL(7, 2),
    OUT p_protein DECIMAL(6, 2),
    OUT p_carbs DECIMAL(6, 2),
    OUT p_fat DECIMAL(6, 2)
)
BEGIN
    SELECT 
        COALESCE(SUM(f.calories * mi.quantity), 0.00),
        COALESCE(SUM(f.protein * mi.quantity), 0.00),
        COALESCE(SUM(f.carbohydrates * mi.quantity), 0.00),
        COALESCE(SUM(f.fat * mi.quantity), 0.00)
    INTO p_calories, p_protein, p_carbs, p_fat
    FROM meal m
    JOIN meal_item mi ON m.meal_id = mi.meal_id
    JOIN food f ON mi.food_id = f.food_id
    WHERE m.user_id = p_user_id AND m.meal_date = p_date;
END $$
DELIMITER ;
    Test Execution:
    
CALL get_daily_summary(1, '2026-10-18', @cal, @pro, @carb, @fat);
SELECT @cal AS daily_calories, @pro AS daily_protein, @carb AS daily_carbs, @fat AS daily_fat;
    Output:
    daily_calories daily_protein daily_carbs daily_fat
    1395.50 97.45 190.60 33.20

    12.3 SQL Views (DBMS Exp 4 & 5)

    View 1: `daily_nutrition_summary`

    Pre-aggregates nutritional consumption per user per day.

    
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW daily_nutrition_summary AS
SELECT 
    m.user_id,
    m.meal_date,
    COALESCE(SUM(f.calories * mi.quantity), 0) AS daily_calories,
    COALESCE(SUM(f.protein * mi.quantity), 0) AS daily_protein,
    COALESCE(SUM(f.carbohydrates * mi.quantity), 0) AS daily_carbs,
    COALESCE(SUM(f.fat * mi.quantity), 0) AS daily_fat
FROM meal m
LEFT JOIN meal_item mi ON m.meal_id = mi.meal_id
LEFT JOIN food f ON mi.food_id = f.food_id
GROUP BY m.user_id, m.meal_date;
    Test Execution:
    
SELECT * FROM daily_nutrition_summary WHERE user_id = 1;
    Output:
    user_id meal_date daily_calories daily_protein daily_carbs daily_fat
    1 2026-10-18 1395.50 97.45 190.60 33.20

    View 2: `food_category_details`

    Pre-joins food catalog items with their dietary categories, removing redundant join code.

    
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW food_category_details AS
SELECT 
    f.food_id,
    f.food_name,
    c.category_name,
    f.serving_size,
    f.calories,
    f.protein,
    f.carbohydrates,
    f.fat
FROM food f
JOIN food_category c ON f.category_id = c.category_id;
    Test Execution:
    
SELECT food_name, category_name, calories, protein FROM food_category_details LIMIT 5;
    Output:
    food_name category_name calories protein

    Rolled Oats Grains 389.00 16.90
    Grilled Chicken Breast Proteins 165.00 31.00
    Yellow Dal (Cooked) Proteins 116.00 7.30

    12.4 Triggers (DBMS Exp 8)

    Trigger 1: `trg_after_meal_insert` (AFTER INSERT Audit Trigger)

    Automatically creates an audit record in activity_log whenever a new meal transaction is committed.

    
DELIMITER $$
CREATE TRIGGER trg_after_meal_insert
AFTER INSERT ON meal
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO activity_log (user_id, action_taken, log_time)
    VALUES (
        NEW.user_id,
        CONCAT('Logged meal (ID: ', NEW.meal_id, ', Type: ', NEW.meal_type, ', Date: ', NEW.meal_date, ')'),
        NOW()
    );
END $$
DELIMITER ;
    Test Execution:
    
INSERT INTO meal (user_id, meal_type, meal_date) VALUES (1, 'Snack', '2026-10-18');
SELECT * FROM activity_log WHERE user_id = 1 ORDER BY log_id DESC LIMIT 1;
    Output:
    log_id user_id action_taken log_time
    5 1 Logged meal (ID: 5, Type: Snack, Date: 2026-10-18) 2026-10-18 23:45:10

    Trigger 2: `trg_validate_meal_quantity` (BEFORE INSERT Validation Trigger)

    Guards the database against non-positive serving quantities by signaling a SQLSTATE error.

    
DELIMITER $$
CREATE TRIGGER trg_validate_meal_quantity
BEFORE INSERT ON meal_item
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
    IF NEW.quantity <= 0 THEN
        SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000'
        SET MESSAGE_TEXT = 'Meal item quantity must be strictly greater than 0';
    END IF;
END $$
DELIMITER ;
    Test Execution:
    
INSERT INTO meal_item (meal_id, food_id, quantity) VALUES (1, 8, -1.00);
    Output:
    
Error Code: 1644. Meal item quantity must be strictly greater than 0 (SQLSTATE 45000)
Query Execution Failed: Insertion Aborted by Trigger.

    Query 1: Top 5 Highest Protein Foods in the Catalog

    Query 2: Aggregate Nutritional Density by Category (GROUP BY, HAVING)

    
SELECT 
    c.category_name,
    COUNT(f.food_id) AS total_food_items,
    ROUND(AVG(f.calories), 2) AS avg_calories,
    ROUND(AVG(f.protein), 2) AS avg_protein
FROM food_category c
JOIN food f ON c.category_id = f.category_id
GROUP BY c.category_id, c.category_name
HAVING COUNT(f.food_id) > 1
ORDER BY avg_calories DESC;
    category_name total_food_items avg_calories avg_protein
    Grains 3 213.00 7.70
    Proteins 4 156.00 15.73
    Dairy 2 60.00 6.60
    Fruits 3 62.67 0.77
    Vegetables 3 47.33 1.83

    Query 3: Multi-Table Intake Breakdown by Meal Type for User 1

    
SELECT 
    m.meal_type,
    COUNT(mi.meal_item_id) AS items_consumed,
    ROUND(SUM(f.calories * mi.quantity), 2) AS total_meal_calories,
    ROUND(SUM(f.protein * mi.quantity), 2) AS total_meal_protein
FROM meal m
JOIN meal_item mi ON m.meal_id = mi.meal_id
JOIN food f ON mi.food_id = f.food_id
WHERE m.user_id = 1 AND m.meal_date = '2026-10-18'
GROUP BY m.meal_id, m.meal_type;
    meal_type items_consumed total_meal_calories total_meal_protein
    Breakfast 3 634.00 30.60
    Lunch 3 462.50 51.75
    Dinner 2 356.00 14.30

    Query 4: Daily Intake vs. Active Target Goal Comparison (CASE Evaluation)

    
SELECT 
    u.name,
    g.target_calories,
    s.daily_calories,
    (s.daily_calories - g.target_calories) AS calorie_variance,
    CASE 
        WHEN s.daily_calories > g.target_calories THEN 'Caloric Surplus'
        WHEN s.daily_calories < g.target_calories THEN 'Caloric Deficit'
        ELSE 'Exact Target Reached'
    END AS status
FROM user_profile u
JOIN nutrition_goal g ON u.user_id = g.user_id AND g.is_active = TRUE
JOIN daily_nutrition_summary s ON u.user_id = s.user_id AND s.meal_date = '2026-10-18'
WHERE u.user_id = 1;
    name target_calories daily_calories calorie_variance status
    John Doe 2200.00 1395.50 -804.50 Caloric Deficit

    Query 5: Unconsumed Food Items in Catalog (LEFT JOIN with IS NULL)

    Identifies reference foods that have never been consumed in any logged meal:

    
SELECT f.food_id, f.food_name, c.category_name
FROM food f
JOIN food_category c ON f.category_id = c.category_id
LEFT JOIN meal_item mi ON f.food_id = mi.food_id
WHERE mi.meal_item_id IS NULL;
    food_id food_name category_name
    6 Fresh Paneer Proteins
    8 Apple Fruits
    10 Orange Fruits
    11 Whole Milk Dairy
    12 Greek Yogurt Dairy
    13 Steamed Broccoli Vegetables
    15 Boiled Potato Vegetables

    Query 6: Foods with Above-Average Caloric Content (Subquery)

    
SELECT food_name, calories
FROM food
WHERE calories > (SELECT AVG(calories) FROM food)
ORDER BY calories DESC;
    food_name calories
    Rolled Oats 389.00
    Fresh Paneer 265.00
    Grilled Chicken Breast 165.00
    Cooked White Rice 130.00
    Whole Wheat Roti 120.00
    Yellow Dal (Cooked) 116.00

    Query 7: Correlated Subquery — Users Consuming More Than 1000 kcal Today

    
SELECT u.user_id, u.name, u.email
FROM user_profile u
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 
    FROM daily_nutrition_summary s 
    WHERE s.user_id = u.user_id 
      AND s.meal_date = '2026-10-18' 
      AND s.daily_calories > 1000.00
);
    user_id name email
    1 John Doe user@example.com

    Query 8: String Formatting of Food Descriptions (String Functions)

    
SELECT 
    food_id,
    UPPER(food_name) AS upper_food,
    CONCAT(food_name, ' [', serving_size, 'g / ', calories, ' kcal]') AS food_label

    13. Application of Codd's 12 Rules

    Dr. E. F. Codd formulated twelve rules (plus Rule 0) that establish whether an information management system qualifies as a true relational database. The NutriGuide system, running on MySQL 8.x with the InnoDB storage engine, is evaluated below against each of Codd's foundational rules:

    Rule No. Rule Name Formal Statement Evaluation in NutriGuide Compliance Status
    Rule 0 Foundation Rule The system must be able to manage databases entirely through its relational capabilities. NutriGuide manages all entities (users, goals, meals, foods, plans, recommendations, audit logs) exclusively through relational tables, keys, and SQL operations. Followed
    Rule 1 Information Rule All information in the database is represented explicitly at the logical level in exactly one way: by values in tables. Every domain fact (from user demographics to portion quantities and trigger audit records) is stored exclusively in rows and columns across the 10 relational tables. Followed
    Rule 2 Guaranteed Access Rule Each and every datum in a relational database is guaranteed to be logically accessible by resorting to a combination of table name, primary key value, and column name. Any specific nutrient or demographic attribute can be directly pinpointed. For example: `SELECT protein FROM food WHERE food_id = 4;` unambiguously retrieves `31.00`. Followed
    Rule 3 Systematic Treatment of NULL Values NULL values are supported in a systematic way, representing missing information or inapplicable data, independent of data type. Columns like `activity_level` allow NULL only when unspecified, whereas mandatory attributes (`name`, `email`, `serving_size`) enforce `NOT NULL`. Null handling functions (`COALESCE`, `IFNULL`) are systematically used. Followed
    Rule 4 Dynamic Online Catalog Based on the Relational Model The database description is represented at the logical level in the same way as ordinary data, so authorized users can query it using relational SQL. Schema metadata is queried relationally via MySQL's `information_schema` (e.g., `SELECT * FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'nutriguide';`). Followed
    Rule 5 Comprehensive Data Sublanguage Rule A relational system may support several languages, but must support at least one well-defined sublanguage supporting DDL, DML, integrity constraints, and transaction control. NutriGuide utilizes SQL for DDL (`CREATE TABLE`), DML (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`), view/trigger declarations, and transaction control (`START TRANSACTION`, `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`). Followed
    Rule 6 View Updating Rule All views that are theoretically updatable are also updatable by the system. Simple views are updatable in MySQL. However, complex aggregation views (`daily_nutrition_summary` with `SUM`, `GROUP BY`, and joins) are non-updatable in MySQL InnoDB, as is standard practice. Partially Followed
    Rule 7 High-Level Insert, Update, and Delete The system must support set-at-a-time operations for retrieval, insertion, update, and deletion, not merely record-at-a-time processing. Bulk operations operate seamlessly on entire tuple sets (e.g., multi-row `INSERT INTO food VALUES (...)`, mass status updates via `UPDATE nutrition_goal SET is_active = FALSE`). Followed
    Rule 8 Physical Data Independence Application programs and terminal activities remain logically unimpaired whenever any changes are made in storage representations or access methods. The physical tablespace layout, B-Tree index structures, and disk allocations are managed entirely by the InnoDB engine without altering application SQL queries. Followed
    Rule 9 Logical Data Independence Application programs and terminal activities remain logically unimpaired when information-preserving changes of any kind that theoretically permit un-impairment are made to the tables. Pre-aggregated SQL views (`daily_nutrition_summary`, `food_category_details`) insulate the application layer from table schema evolutions, though drastic structural changes may require query updates. Partially Followed
    Rule 10 Integrity Independence Integrity constraints must be definable in the relational data sublanguage and stored in the catalog, not in application programs. All constraints (PKs, FKs with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, `CHECK` bounds on heights/weights, `UNIQUE` email keys, and triggers) reside directly inside MySQL, not in client code. Followed
    Rule 11 Distribution Independence The data manipulation sublanguage of a relational DBMS must enable application programs to remain unchanged whether data is centralized or distributed. NutriGuide operates on a centralized MySQL 8.x database server; distributed transparency (e.g., two-phase commit over sharded nodes) is not implemented. Not Applicable
    Rule 12 Non-Subversion Rule If a relational system has a low-level language, that low level cannot be used to subvert or bypass the integrity rules and constraints. Access to MySQL storage is strictly mediated via SQL under authentication privileges. Engine constraints cannot be bypassed by low-level row manipulations. Followed

    15. Conclusion

    The NutriGuide relational database project successfully demonstrates the end-to-end design, normalization, implementation, and optimization of an academic and clinical-grade personal nutrition management database.

    Key Project Achievements:

  • Pristine 3NF / BCNF Schema: By decomposing the unnormalized flat meal model into ten discrete relational tables, all insertion, update, and deletion anomalies were formally eliminated.
  • Associative Relationship Resolution: Many-to-many cardinalities between meals and foods, as well as meal plans and foods, were cleanly resolved via associative junction entities with portion quantities.
  • Rigorous Referential Integrity: Explicit foreign key actions (CASCADE on user dependents, RESTRICT on catalog items) guarantee that historical dietary logs remain permanent and audit-compliant.
  • Declarative Database Constraints: Boundary rules on physical dimensions, caloric targets, and serving portions are enforced at the database kernel level through CHECK constraints and NOT NULL rules.
  • Advanced Database Programmability: The inclusion of stored functions (dynamic BMI evaluation), stored procedures (consolidated daily summaries with OUT parameters), views (pre-aggregated daily totals), and triggers (automated audit trails and SQLSTATE validation) highlights the power of modern database engines.

    • The project demonstrates compliance with the B.Tech Computer Science DBMS curriculum standards, illustrating how relational theory directly translates into reliable, scalable software engineering.

    • Appendix A. Complete SQL Script (`NutriGuide.sql`)

    
-- ============================================================================
-- NutriGuide Database Schema: Complete DDL & Baseline Data
-- Database Engine: MySQL 8.x | Storage Engine: InnoDB
-- ============================================================================

CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS nutriguide;
USE nutriguide;

-- Table 1: user_profile
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS user_profile (
    user_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    password_hash VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    age INT NOT NULL CHECK (age > 0),
    gender VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    height_cm DECIMAL(5, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (height_cm > 0),
    weight_kg DECIMAL(5, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (weight_kg > 0),
    activity_level VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- Table 2: nutrition_goal
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS nutrition_goal (
    goal_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INT NOT NULL,
    target_calories DECIMAL(7, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (target_calories >= 0),
    target_protein DECIMAL(6, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (target_protein >= 0),
    target_carbs DECIMAL(6, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (target_carbs >= 0),
    target_fats DECIMAL(6, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (target_fats >= 0),
    is_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    CONSTRAINT fk_nutrition_goal_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
        REFERENCES user_profile (user_id)
        ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- Table 3: food_category
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS food_category (
    category_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    category_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- Table 4: food
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS food (
    food_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    category_id INT NOT NULL,
    food_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    serving_size DECIMAL(6, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (serving_size > 0),
    calories DECIMAL(6, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (calories >= 0),
    protein DECIMAL(5, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (protein >= 0),
    carbohydrates DECIMAL(5, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (carbohydrates >= 0),
    fat DECIMAL(5, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (fat >= 0),
    CONSTRAINT fk_food_category FOREIGN KEY (category_id)
        REFERENCES food_category (category_id)
        ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- Table 5: meal
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS meal (
    meal_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INT NOT NULL,
    meal_type VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    meal_date DATE NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    CONSTRAINT fk_meal_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
        REFERENCES user_profile (user_id)
        ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- Table 6: meal_item
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS meal_item (
    meal_item_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    meal_id INT NOT NULL,
    food_id INT NOT NULL,
    quantity DECIMAL(5, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
    CONSTRAINT fk_meal_item_meal FOREIGN KEY (meal_id)
        REFERENCES meal (meal_id)
        ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE,
    CONSTRAINT fk_meal_item_food FOREIGN KEY (food_id)
        REFERENCES food (food_id)
        ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- Table 7: meal_plan
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS meal_plan (
    meal_plan_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INT NOT NULL,
    plan_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    start_date DATE NOT NULL,
    end_date DATE NOT NULL,
    is_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    CONSTRAINT fk_meal_plan_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
        REFERENCES user_profile (user_id)
        ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- Table 8: meal_plan_item
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS meal_plan_item (
    meal_plan_item_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    meal_plan_id INT NOT NULL,
    food_id INT NOT NULL,
    planned_meal_type VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    quantity DECIMAL(5, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
    CONSTRAINT fk_meal_plan_item_plan FOREIGN KEY (meal_plan_id)
        REFERENCES meal_plan (meal_plan_id)
        ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE,
    CONSTRAINT fk_meal_plan_item_food FOREIGN KEY (food_id)
        REFERENCES food (food_id)
        ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- Table 9: recommendation
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS recommendation (
    rec_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INT NOT NULL,
    rec_type VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    message VARCHAR(500) NOT NULL,
    generated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    CONSTRAINT fk_recommendation_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
        REFERENCES user_profile (user_id)
        ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- Table 10: activity_log
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS activity_log (
    log_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INT NOT NULL,
    action_taken VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    log_time TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    CONSTRAINT fk_activity_log_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
        REFERENCES user_profile (user_id)
        ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

    Appendix B. Stored Routines & Test Suite

    
USE nutriguide;

-- Views
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW daily_nutrition_summary AS
SELECT 
    m.user_id,
    m.meal_date,
    COALESCE(SUM(f.calories * mi.quantity), 0) AS daily_calories,
    COALESCE(SUM(f.protein * mi.quantity), 0) AS daily_protein,
    COALESCE(SUM(f.carbohydrates * mi.quantity), 0) AS daily_carbs,
    COALESCE(SUM(f.fat * mi.quantity), 0) AS daily_fat
FROM meal m
LEFT JOIN meal_item mi ON m.meal_id = mi.meal_id
LEFT JOIN food f ON mi.food_id = f.food_id
GROUP BY m.user_id, m.meal_date;

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW food_category_details AS
SELECT 
    f.food_id,
    f.food_name,
    c.category_name,
    f.serving_size,
    f.calories,
    f.protein,
    f.carbohydrates,
    f.fat
FROM food f
JOIN food_category c ON f.category_id = c.category_id;

-- Stored Functions
DELIMITER $$
CREATE FUNCTION calculate_bmi(weight_kg DECIMAL(5, 2), height_cm DECIMAL(5, 2))
RETURNS DECIMAL(5, 2)
DETERMINISTIC NO SQL
BEGIN
    DECLARE height_m DECIMAL(5, 4);
    IF height_cm IS NULL OR height_cm <= 0 OR weight_kg IS NULL OR weight_kg <= 0 THEN
        RETURN 0.00;
    END IF;
    SET height_m = height_cm / 100.0000;
    RETURN ROUND(weight_kg / (height_m * height_m), 2);
END $$

CREATE FUNCTION get_total_calories(p_user_id INT, p_date DATE)
RETURNS DECIMAL(7, 2)
READS SQL DATA
BEGIN
    DECLARE total_cals DECIMAL(7, 2);
    SELECT COALESCE(SUM(f.calories * mi.quantity), 0.00)
    INTO total_cals
    FROM meal m
    JOIN meal_item mi ON m.meal_id = mi.meal_id
    JOIN food f ON mi.food_id = f.food_id
    WHERE m.user_id = p_user_id AND m.meal_date = p_date;
    RETURN total_cals;
END $$

-- Stored Procedure
CREATE PROCEDURE get_daily_summary(
    IN p_user_id INT,
    IN p_date DATE,
    OUT p_calories DECIMAL(7, 2),
    OUT p_protein DECIMAL(6, 2),
    OUT p_carbs DECIMAL(6, 2),
    OUT p_fat DECIMAL(6, 2)
)
BEGIN
    SELECT 
        COALESCE(SUM(f.calories * mi.quantity), 0.00),
        COALESCE(SUM(f.protein * mi.quantity), 0.00),
        COALESCE(SUM(f.carbohydrates * mi.quantity), 0.00),
        COALESCE(SUM(f.fat * mi.quantity), 0.00)
    INTO p_calories, p_protein, p_carbs, p_fat
    FROM meal m
    JOIN meal_item mi ON m.meal_id = mi.meal_id
    JOIN food f ON mi.food_id = f.food_id
    WHERE m.user_id = p_user_id AND m.meal_date = p_date;
END $$

-- Triggers
CREATE TRIGGER trg_after_meal_insert
AFTER INSERT ON meal
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO activity_log (user_id, action_taken, log_time)
    VALUES (
        NEW.user_id,
        CONCAT('Logged meal (ID: ', NEW.meal_id, ', Type: ', NEW.meal_type, ', Date: ', NEW.meal_date, ')'),
        NOW()
    );
END $$

CREATE TRIGGER trg_validate_meal_quantity
BEFORE INSERT ON meal_item
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
    IF NEW.quantity <= 0 THEN
        SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000'
        SET MESSAGE_TEXT = 'Meal item quantity must be strictly greater than 0';
    END IF;
END $$
DELIMITER ;
